WHEN THEY RISE
Source: BNP Paribas, Bloomberg
Equity Focus

Summary
1. It Takes Two To Tango – rising yields have not weighed  
on equities. This may look counterintuitive at the first 
glance  but can be explained by superior earnings 
growth. If earnings outgrow rates, equities remain 
attractive. We also don´t see evidence of large 
reallocations into bonds. We remain overweight equities. 
Continuous upward revisions to EPS growth forecasts are 
a key pillar of the bull market. 
2. Kissed By The Muse – Earnings momentum in the US 
remains exceptionally strong as the AI infrastructure 
buildout is increasingly met by rising demand from 
corporate and private users. We upgrade US equities and 
Information Technology to overweight and recommend 
fading US large-cap and Hyperscalers underweights. The 
combination of emerging (Agentic) AI monetization 
avenues, resilient business models, and solid earnings/ 
improving cash flows at hyperscalers has bolstered our 
confidence in their expected free cash flow (FCF) 
recovery (likely within 12-24 months). 
3. We turn neutral on US small versus large caps and 
no longer prefer the equal-weighted S&P 500 over its 
cap-weighted counterpart . 
4. Europe - The Weakest Link - While the headwinds for 
European equities remain plentiful, tailwinds are harder 
to 
find. 
We 
downgrade 
European 
equities 
to 
underweight not because we´re outright bearish but 
because we feel it is the weakest link in our coverage 
and is most likely to trail global peers. At this point, 
Europe remains a place for stock picking, not for owing 
broad market exposure 
5. European banks are downgraded to Neutral and 
European Technology is upgraded to Overweight - 
rising inflation, yields and political issues could hurt 
banking businesses and push investors to book some 
profits. Wait for a more stable environment before re-
entering European banks and/or buy on dips.

CHART 2: G BEATS R – EARNINGS ARE RISING 
FASTER THAN RATES
Source: BNP Paribas, Bloomberg 
2
One of 2026’s more remarkable outcomes is that equities 
have rallied alongside rising yields. Yet global equities are 
up about 13% even as the US 10-year Treasury yield has 
climbed 100bp. These figures sit in an uneasy tension. 
Higher bond yields both increase the returns available 
elsewhere and the discount rate applied to future profits, 
theoretically reducing equity valuations. But it takes two 
to tango. Under the Gordon Growth model, a stock’s value 
equals expected dividends (D) divided by r − g, where r is 
the required return and g is growth. Higher rates raise r 
and weigh on valuations; however, stronger growth lifts 
g and works in the opposite direction. The key is not r 
alone, but the gap between the two. 
The equation is algebraic, but psychology still matters. 
When rates rise amid strong market conditions, investors 
may increase their expectations for future growth, g, 
even faster. We believe that is exactly what has 
happened. Using the US 10-year yield as the best global 
proxy for the risk-free rate (r), earnings growth (g) has 
been stronger in every region except Europe, where year-
to-date EPS growth has lagged the rise in Treasury and 
Bund yields (Chart 2).
A resilient equity risk premium
Had you told investors on January 1 that the S&P 500 
would gain 13% while the US 10-year yield rose 100bp, 
they would reasonably have expected the equity risk 
premium (ERP) to fall significantly. But strong earnings 
have kept the gap between the S&P 500 earnings yield 
and Treasury yields, despite the recent drop, broadly 
unchanged year-to-date (Chart 3). 
Earnings, not multiple expansion, are driving this year’s 
gains. 
Are higher rates prompting investors to reallocate?
Today’s higher-yielding bonds are highly liquid and 
accessible 
to 
global 
investors. 
Whatever 
relative 
valuations imply on paper, investors selling equities or 
other assets to buy bonds would show that the yield 
advantage is compelling enough to change allocations.
So far, however, there is little evidence of such a shift. 
ETF flows, a useful gauge because they respond quickly, 
remain positive for US equities and have already 
surpassed last year’s inflows (Chart 4). Moreover, bonds 
and equities have generally moved in the same direction, 
showing positive correlation—the opposite of what we 
would expect if investors were shifting meaningfully 
from one to the other (Chart 5).
Don´ t fear the Mid-Terms
Another reason which worries investors and appears to 
keep sentiment low (Charts 6 + 7) are the upcoming US 
mid-term elections. While the outcome could trigger 
increased volatility at a sector level, history suggests that 
equities are only impacted for a limited period. Since 
1950, the S&P 500 gained an average of 16.7% in the 12 
months following the mid-terms and was higher on 
every occasion (Chart 8). Moreover, seasonality is 
changing from a headwind to a tailwind with October 
being the strongest month in a mid-term year on 
average (Chart 9). This supports our equity overweight 
thesis and – alongside further AI tailwinds - our upgrade 
of US equities to overweight.

CHART 10: GUIDANCE UPGRADES ARE 
STRONG AS WE HEAD INTO Q3 EARNINGS
Source: BNP Paribas, Factset 
4
Earnings momentum in the US remains exceptionally 
strong. Revisions of earnings growth for 2026 since 
January 1st are the second strongest within the last 15 
years (Chart 12). This optimism among investors is fueled 
by ongoing optimism among companies. As we enter the 
Q3 earnings season, 116 S&P 500 constituents have 
issued EPS guidance. Out of these companies, 62% (72  
out of 116) have issued positive guidance which scores 
well above the 5-year (40%) and 10-year (41%) average. 
Looking into sectors, Technology is leading with 44 
upgrades, almost double the 5-year average (Charts 10 & 
11). Overall, EPS for the S&P 500 is expected to grow by 
~35% yoy in Q3 which, if realized, would mark the 3rd 
consecutive quarter with earnings growth above 30% and 
the 8th consecutive quarter with double digit earnings 
growth (Chart 13).
A key driver of earnings remain Artificial Intelligence. 
The S&P 500 ex AI has decoupled from the S&P 500 
alongside slower EPS growth expectations (Charts 14 & 
15). However, looking at ongoing strong PMI data, we 
think that it is more likely that we will see non-tech 
catching up higher rather than the other way around. 
Our commodity strategist continues to expect oil prices 
(Brent) to decline to USD65/barrel within 12 months, 
allowing the Fed to follow a less aggressive hiking path. 
Our two expected rate hikes are still well below the 
current market pricing of c. 3.5 hikes by December 2027. 
Taken with our 12-month US 10-year yield forecast of 
4.75%, we think the market is currently too pessimistic 
about the prospects of Corporate America as a whole.
Rates are a small (cap) problem
Rising rates are thus far having only a small impact on 
the rates burden of corporates at least when looking at 
net interest payments as a % of US-GDP (Chart 16). This 
is mainly due to a lot of long-term borrowing by 
companies during the low-rate era. Thus, interest rate 
expenses as % of revenues for companies within the S&P 
500 have barely moved. The same cannot be said about 
small caps. Since 2022, the interest rate burden has risen 
constantly as small caps rely much more on short-dated 
debt than their larger peers (Charts 17 & 18). Thus, the 
Russell 2000 historically fell around 10% during the first 
weeks after a Fed rate hike (Chart 19). Since the relative 
performance of the Russell 2000 vs the S&P 500 has so 
far defied the move in rates (Chart 20), we see a high 
risk of major underperformance going forward. 
We upgrade US equities and, globally, Technology to 
overweight and recommend reducing US large-cap 
underweights. We turn neutral on US small versus large 
caps and no longer prefer the equal-weighted S&P 500 
over its cap-weighted counterpart. 
Kissed by the Muse
AI remains top of mind for company executives, leading 
to rising applied AI maturity scores. These  scores look to 
measure AI capabilities of companies and underline a 
strong acceleration during the last year alongside 
growing AI-related investment. One factor motivating 
executives are the expected benefits from solid AI 
adoption rates on revenues and costs (Charts 20 & 21).

CHART 24: TALKING ABOUT AI IS WELL 
RECEIVED BY INVESTORS
Source: BNP Paribas, Factset
CHART 23: THE BENEFITS FROM EMPLOYING 
AI ARE RISING
Source: BNP Paribas, BCG
7
Transiting from the laggard cohort in 2025 into the 
future-built cohort in 2030 can amplify the positive 
effects from AI on costs and revenue by a factor of 10 
(Chart 23). Those efforts are also increasingly appreciated 
by the market as the stocks of companies talking about AI 
in their earnings calls materially outperformed both in Q2 
2026 and year-to-date (Chart 24). This strengthens our 
case for remaining positive on AI infrastructure names as 
rising revenues should maintain AI buildout momentum. 
Another driver of growing demand for compute – and 
everything related to it, ranging from power to 
datacenters – is the rising use of Agentic AI. By 2030, the 
share of Agentic AI is expected to rise by c. 77% vs 2026 
(Chart 25). This is important as AI agents use 
exponentially more tokens than non-agentic AI. Agentic 
workloads can consume roughly 100 times more tokens 
than conversational chat interactions. This increase is 
driven by the complexity of planning, memory 
requirements, and tool orchestration. Token usage data 
from openrouter.ai confirms this observation as Agentic 
AI strongly outgrew human token usage (Chart 26).
Agentic AI won´t be limited to corporate usage though. 
The recent launch of Meta´s “muse” is a major 
achievement in private agentic AI usage. The app quickly 
climbed the ranks in App stores and reached 5 million 
downloads within 22 days. For reference, it took ChatGPT 
56 days to reach the same number of downloads. While 
this success lifted Agentic related sectors exposed to the 
agentic AI buildout - infrastructure, (cybersecurity) 
software, and enablers that benefit from AI agents 
replacing or augmenting human workflows – it is 
perceived as a disruptive force for others (Chart 27).
Goodbye inertia?
AI agents improve price comparison, trip booking and 
dealing with customer service interactions. Hence, 
industries that rely on recurring bills, negotiable pricing 
and add-ons are facing increasing pressure. Historically, 
customers are rarely revisiting their existing contracts, a 
phenomena called “consumer inertia”. As AI agents are 
now able to renegotiate contracts and switch/cancel 
services, it might get harder for companies to benefit 
from “lazy” consumers. 
Since its launch, there were no shortage of Muse posts in 
social media on how to lower and cancel a subscription 
service that has sat idle for months. To what extend this 
will have a notable impact on earnings needs to be 
monitored though. Thus far, only a limited share of 
consumers said they would be comfortable with AI 
choosing and purchasing things on their behalf while 
42% of the respondents declared that they would not 
trust AI to make purchases on their behalf (Chart 28). 
The same survey also revealed that AI is becoming 
increasingly important in selecting products (Chart 29). 
This confirm the potential positive revenue impact of AI 
advertisement for vendors which we discussed here.
Japan – remaining a key AI call
The definition of an “AI-related stock” has broadened 
considerably in recent years. The AI theme now extends 
far beyond processors and semiconductor equipment to 
include 
optical 
interconnects, 
power 
and 
cooling 
infrastructure, robotics, and applications. Japan is home 
to many leading companies in this space and is well 
poised to benefit from the broadening of the theme. We 
reiterate our overweight rating, preferably played via the 
Nikkei 225 due to its higher AI exposure (Chart 30).

Europe – the weakest link
Europe continues to suffer form a variety of headwinds. 
Energy prices remain high and will most likely keep 
weighing on consumption and corporate margins. 
Moreover, water levels in the river Rhine continued to 
fall in the recent weeks due to a lag of rain . At the time 
of writing, no ships can pass Kaub, a critical chokepoint 
in south-western Germany. This will have a negative 
impact on manufacturing, as we discussed here. We 
therefore believe that the decline in industrial orders of 
10,6% in August might be only a harbinger of more 
weakness to come (Chart 31).
Another factor weighing on European equities are 
increasing bond yields and spreads against German 
bunds because of growing political risks in several 
countries of the Eurozone (Chart 32). Financials, which 
are holding a decent amount of those bonds, are suffering 
as a result and are turning from market leaders to 
market laggers (Chart 33).
While the headwinds for European equities remain 
plentiful, tailwinds are harder to find. The region lacks 
the structural exposure to AI infrastructure which we 
find elsewhere. The main argument in favor of Europe 
seems to be the price. Despite the rerating over the last 
18 months, the region´s valuation remains below its 
long-term average ratio to global stocks (Chart 34). Even 
if 
we 
discount 
for 
some 
potential 
earnings 
disappointments, this should provide some cushion 
against a major drawdown. 
We downgrade European equities to underweight not 
because we  are outright bearish but because we feel it is 
the weakest link in our coverage and is most likely to 
trail global peers. At this point, Europe remains a place for 
stock picking, not for owing broad market exposure.

CHART 35 : US SECTOR PERFORMANCE (AS OF 
30TH OF SEPT.): ENERGY, IT AND HEALTH 
CARE LEADING; FINANCIALS, CONSUMER 
DISCR. & UTILITIES AT THE BOTTOM.  
                 Source: S&P 500, 2026 performances as at 30th of Sept. 2026. 
10
US equities : breaking new ground
The US tech sector kicked off 2026 strongly but paused 
for consolidation over the summer. Meanwhile, broader 
market leadership rotated, with the S&P 500 hitting fresh 
all-time highs in August before moving sideways again.
Key headwinds—rising oil prices, climbing bond yields, 
and seasonal weakness—weighed on sentiment. While 
Q2 earnings were exceptionally robust, investors grew 
cautious, questioning whether the rally had fully priced 
in positive developments. Yet, the US economy continues 
to defy expectations, displaying resilience and relatively 
controlled inflation, while corporate earnings forecasts 
keep trending upward.
Now, US equities have regained momentum, propelled by 
strong tech-sector fundamentals: companies across the 
board are upwardly revising revenue, earnings, and cash 
flow guidance, reigniting bullish sentiment.
The launch of new monetizable agentic AI assistants—
such as Meta’s Muse, ChatGPT Dots, and consumer-
focused Copilot upgrades—has fed the momentum in the 
tech sector (cf. Meta Platforms gaining +26,7% in 
September). 
Information Technology and Communication Services 
each advanced c. 4% in September (the only US sectors in 
positive territory), while the S&P 500 dipped -0.45% over 
the month. Healthcare (-1%) and Energy (-2.8%) fared 
best among laggards.
Year-to-date, the S&P 500 remains up +11.8%, led by 
Energy (+37.4%), Information Technology (+27.9%), and 
Healthcare (+8.8%).
Global Overweight on Information Technology
The combination of emerging (Agentic) AI monetization 
avenues, resilient business models, and solid earnings/ 
improving cash flows at hyperscalers has bolstered our 
confidence in their expected free cash flow (FCF) 
recovery. As a result, we are fading our hyperscalers’ 
underweight recommendation, particularly as valuations 
now sit at the lower end of their range (Chart 36). That 
said, we advocate a selective approach: focus on names 
with robust balance sheets and clear pathways to rising 
FCF generation.
Semiconductors remain attractive, now also trading at 
compelling valuations. Combined with opportunities in 
tech hardware, cybersecurity, software and services 
(strong recovery of this sub-sector since mid-July), we 
are upgrading US Information Technology from Neutral to 
Overweight. 
For 
other 
tech-exposed 
sectors 
like 
Communication Services and Consumer Discretionary, we 
maintain a Neutral stance due to disruptive pressures—
e.g., SpaceX’s telecom push, US firms facing stiff Chinese 
competition in discretionary goods, etc. In Europe, tech 
indices have also broken out to new highs. Given their 
strong outlook, we are also upgrading our rating on 
European tech from Neutral to Overweight.
Globally, we recommend an Overweight on IT as we also 
like Japanese, South Korean, Taiwanese and some parts of 
Chinese tech. Note, however, that Korea faces short-term 
headwinds from renewed geopolitical tensions and 
potentially new Chinese competition in memory chips.

Europe 
Falling 
Behind : 
Structural 
Weaknesses 
Weigh on Performance
Over the past few years, Europe has followed a 
frustratingly consistent pattern: a promising start to the 
year, only to lose momentum as global trends shift. In 
2026, this dynamic has repeated itself, with European 
markets now lagging other regions. The root causes are 
clear: the continent remains underexposed to the AI and 
technology 
themes 
driving 
global 
growth, 
while 
persistently high energy and labour costs continue to 
undermine industrial competitiveness. Adding to these 
challenges, resurgent inflation and rising bond yields and 
a sharp widening in the spread between French OATs and 
German Bunds, reflecting heightened market stress.
Given these headwinds—both structural and cyclical—
we anticipate that European equities will struggle to 
outperform. Against this backdrop, we are downgrading 
the European banking sector from Overweight to Neutral, 
despite its undemanding valuation (forward P/E of 10.2x). 
The current uncertainties and profit-taking pressures—
after years of strong performance (cf. chart 38) — lead us 
to a more cautious stance.
In September, only Energy (+2.8%) and Technology (+2%) 
ended the month in positive territory. On a YTD basis, 
Energy (+34.7%), Technology (+23.8%), Basic Resources 
(+21.7%), and Banks (+18.9%) remain the top performers 
(chart 37). Currently, we favour sectors displaying solid 
earnings, robust order books, pricing power, and 
improving cash flows— cf. upgrade of US and European IT 
to OW. Conversely, high(er) interest rates and energy 
prices could weigh on economic/ lending activity, leading 
us to tactically downgrade EU banks from OW to N.
Q3-26 Earnings Outlook – Information Technology 
expected to deliver a whopping +67% EPS growth!
Major equity markets have reached new highs this year. 
But the real story lies in their fundamentals: earnings 
growth has significantly outpaced price appreciation, 
resulting in more attractive valuations (chart 1). As a 
reminder, S&P 500 2026 EPS is expected to rise by +30% 
whereas the index has progressed by ‘only’ +11.8% this 
year, diminishing its forward P/E to a reasonable 19x. 
Even more striking is the projected earnings growth of 
the Mag-7: +52% whereas non-tech stocks should grow 
EPS by +22% in 2026. Meanwhile, Europe and Japan are 
forecast earnings growth of slightly over 15%, with China 
trailing behind. The most notable outperformance, 
however, is expected in emerging markets, where 
earnings are projected to surge by +67%, largely fueled 
by the strong contributions of South Korea and Taiwan.
For Q3-2026, analysts’ consensus forecasts close to +30% 
earnings growth in the US. Revenues are expected  to rise 
by an exceptionally high +12%, led by IT’s +40% forecast 
increase. As usual, hyperscalers’ results - their (expected) 
cash flows in particular - will be closely scrutinized, given 
their pivotal role in both the AI-driven capex boom and 
overall US earnings growth.
The IT sector is poised to deliver an exceptional earnings 
growth of +67%. By comparison, non-tech sectors are 
projected to grow EPS by +22%. Consumer-related sectors 
will likely report the weakest performance (+3%). In 
Europe, Q3 EPS growth is forecasted at +22%, once again 
driven by Energy, Financials, Industrials and Technology.
